newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, munis best bets for investor -- Nuveen study.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, munis best bets for investor -- Nuveen study.

text.p: An "extensive" study by John Nuveen & Co focusing on mid-1970s to mid-1990s found that equities and municipal bonds provided the best return for investors after taxes and inflation, Nuveen's director of research said.

Paul Williams, a vice president and manager of Nuveen's Investment Strategies and Research group, said in a recent interview with Reuters that while the findings didn't surprise him, the confirmation was heartening.
While equities outperformed munis, on an after-tax basis munis "very clearly" outperformed other assets such as governments, and corporates and Treasury bills, Williams said.

Armed with that information, Nuveen launched three new funds, designed to broaden investment opportunities for the conservative investor Nuveen serves. An all equities fund called Nuveen Growth and Income Stock Fund raised $475 million during the load-waived offering period for Nuveen investors that began in September. The fund was offered to the public Feb 1.

The two other funds -- Nuveen Balanced Stock and Bond Fund and Nuveen Balanced Municipal and Stock Fund -- are now available in a load-waived offering period for Nuveen Investors. Chicago-based Institutional Capital Corp serves as sub-adviser on the equity portion.

A look at the behavior of a balance portfolio on an after-tax basis reveals that fixed-income securities in general, and municipals in particular, can help reduce the volatility of returns and asset values, Williams said.

While investors who recently bought a 5-1/4 percent to 5-1/2 percent longer term municipal bond might feel "stuck with it" because they have seen little appreciation, "they've still had a very good after-tax yield against inflation during this period," Williams said.
"So they in fact made an investment that had economic value, they just haven't had a lot of flexibility with it if they are motivated to trade," he said.

Conversely, if an investor buys a bond yielding 5-1/4 percent, and the market backs off to a 6.0 percent yield, the investor has an opportunity to use the loss to write off taxable gains in the stock market in addition to picking up income returns anyway.

"So there are a lot of strategies that you can implement by just watching the balanced relationship between both segments of your portfolio, and I think individual investors are becoming more knowledgeable that those avenues are open to them," he said.
Even an investor who has $50,000 in munis and $100,000 in equities can, using mutual funds, make those maneuvers back and forth," Williams said.
"It may not be as efficient as in the higher bracket, but it still works," Williams said.
